extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of a periodical (coffee-house/early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, public-facing moral and literary essays (Spectator-style) that evaluate behaviours, art, translation, and passions for a literate readership; mixes criticism, moral reflection, and practical examples. Emphasis on instructing manners and taste through examples and aphoristic guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful translation of the Ancients
rubrics_metrics.description: The Compositions of the Ancients ... are extremely difficult to render into another Tongue, so as the Beauties of the Original may not appear weak and faded in the Translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding 'unnatural Witticisms' to please ordinary readers; preserve the beauties and structure of the original (the Ode is cited as a 'Pattern of Perfection in the Structure'). Translators should resist forcing modern conceits that dilute the original's strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous modern witticisms in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Compositions of the Ancients, which have not in them any of those unnatural Witticisms that are the Delight of ordinary Readers, are extremely difficult to render ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce 'unnatural Witticisms' that the original lacks; such insertions make the translated beauties 'weak and faded.' Fidelity to tone and restraint are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition judged by object and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: This Passion ... is frequently perverted to evil and ignoble Purposes; so that we may account for many of the Excellencies and Follies of Life upon the same innate Principle, to wit, the Desire of being remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition is not intrinsically good or bad — evaluate it by its ends (noble/public-spirited vs. selfish/avaricious) and by methods employed (justifiable means vs. cunning/selfishness). Education directs ambition toward valuable objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of ambition: public-spirited vs base
rubrics_metrics.description: It does accordingly express itself in Acts of Magnanimity or selfish Cunning ... As it has been employed in embellishing the Mind, or adorning the Outside, it renders the Man eminently Praise-worthy or ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ambition's manifestation: when it embellishes the mind it is praise-worthy; when it adorns the outside it is often ridiculous. Look to outcomes (benefit to country/society vs. frivolous notoriety).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuousness as a tactic for distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything glaring and particular, either in Behaviour or Apparel, is known to have this good Effect, that it catches the Eye, and will not suffer you to pass over the Person so adorn'd without due Notice and Observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that ostentation and peculiar behaviour function instrumentally to secure notice; treat such tactics as superficial routes to distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of ambition's excess (social anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: To this passionate Fondness for Distinction are owing various frolicksome and irregular Practices, as sallying out into Nocturnal Exploits, breaking of Windows, singing of Catches, beating the Watch, getting Drunk twice a Day, killing a great Number of Horses; with many other Enterprizes of the like fiery Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These behaviors are examples of ambition turned to folly/vanity — use them as cautionary examples when diagnosing social excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avarice as degraded ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: One very Common, and at the same time the most absurd Ambition ... I mean the Passion for getting Money, exclusive of the Character of the Provident Father ... It may be remarked ... that this Desire reigns most in those who have but few good Qualities to recommend them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat covetousness for money (separate from prudent provision) as an inferior, corrupt form of ambition that undermines other virtues and social relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and religion as channels for passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Education determines it to this or that particular Object ... It is the Business of Religion and Philosophy not so much to extinguish our Passions, as to regulate and direct them to valuable well-chosen Objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating character or shaping ambition, emphasize institutions (education, religion, philosophy) that regulate passions toward societally valuable ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion in conversation — selectivity of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The great Difference is that the first knows how to pick and cull his Thoughts for Conversation, by suppressing some, and communicating others; whereas the other lets them all indifferently fly out in Words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good conversational writing/behaviour requires tasteful selection and suppression; indiscriminate self-expression is a mark of folly. Encourage restraint and curation of material in public-facing prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion as a guiding virtue across actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion does not only shew it self in Words, but in all the Circumstances of Action; and is like an Under-Agent of Providence, to guide and direct us in the ordinary Concerns of Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value discretion as the attribute that gives other talents practical effect; in evaluating character or composing moral argument, foreground prudential judgement that orders other qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion vs cunning (ends and methods test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion points out the noblest Ends to us, and pursues the most proper and laudable Methods of attaining them: Cunning has only private selfish Aims, and sticks at nothing which may make them succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate morally between discreet conduct (public-spirited, proper methods) and cunning (selfish, unscrupulous means). Detection of cunning defeats it; discretion builds durable authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership via recognizing others' talents
rubrics_metrics.description: The discreet Man finds out the Talents of those he Converses with, and knows how to apply them to proper Uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social actors by their ability to perceive and deploy the abilities of others; a discreet leader organizes collective talent rather than merely displaying his own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farsightedness and moral calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cast of Mind which is natural to a discreet Man, makes him look forward into Futurity, and consider what will be his Condition Millions of Ages hence, as well as what it is at present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion entails long-term thinking and consideration of distant consequences (including considerations of hereafter); evaluate decisions by their distant as well as immediate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting as a vehicle for moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Art of Painting ... places the Action of the Person represented in the most agreeable Aspect imaginable ... What strong Images of Virtue and Humanity might we not expect would be instill'd into the Mind from the Labours of the Pencil?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privilegiate history/portrait-like paintings that depict real-life virtuous actions as powerful, accessible moral instruction — painting can teach more directly than writing for many viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter selection for moral impact in art
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is the better Man for beholding the most beautiful Venus, the best wrought Bacchanal, the Images of sleeping Cupids ... But if the Virtues and Vices ... were given us by the Painter in the Characters of real Life, and the Persons of Men and Women whose Actions have render'd them laudable or infamous; we should not see a good History-Piece without receiving an instructive Lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects that present virtues/vices through recognizable human characters and actions rather than idealized mythological erotic scenes when the aim is moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual art can convey complex passions more forcefully than prose
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole Work is an Exercise of the highest Piety in the Painter; and all the Touches of a religious Mind are express'd in a Manner much more forcible than can possibly be perform'd by the most moving Eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for art's social value, cite concrete examples (Raphael's Cartoons) where composition, expression, and group dynamics communicate moral and emotional nuance beyond words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and patronize modest foreign merit
rubrics_metrics.description: It is certainly the greatest Honour we can do our Country, to distinguish Strangers of Merit who apply to us with Modesty and Diffidence ... My Skill in Paintings ... makes me at a loss how to mention the Pieces which Mr. Boul exposes to Sale ... commended by those who have bought of him heretofore for great Integrity in his Dealing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage openness to modest, deserving foreign artists; value dealer integrity and modesty in artists when recommending works or fostering national taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule and satire as therapeutic for passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule, perhaps, is a better Expedient against Love than sober Advice, and I am of Opinion, that Hudibras and Don Quixote may be as effectual to cure the Extravagancies of this Passion, as any of the old Philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider satire and comic exemplars as legitimate remedial tools for correcting excessive passions; literary satire can dislodge romantic folly by making it ridiculous.
